objectives: Derive hydrostatic equilibrium from a pressure balance.
Distinguish pp-chain and CNO cycle fusion regimes.
Estimate central conditions from Virial theorem scalings.

slides.title: Stars: gravitationally bound thermonuclear engines
slides.body:
A **star** is a self-gravitating ball of plasma in **hydrostatic equilibrium** — the inward pull of gravity balanced by outward pressure gradient. The Sun: M☉ = 2×10³⁰ kg, R☉ = 7×10⁸ m, L☉ = 3.8×10²⁶ W, T_eff ≈ 5780 K, core T ≈ 1.5×10⁷ K, core ρ ≈ 150 g/cm³. Lifespan on the **main sequence** (MS): the phase where it fuses hydrogen to helium in the core. For the Sun that's ~10 Gyr; the entire universe is only ~13.8 Gyr old, so most low-mass stars ever born are still on the MS.

Four structural equations (1D, spherical): hydrostatic balance dP/dr = −Gm(r)ρ/r², mass continuity dm/dr = 4πr²ρ, energy generation dL/dr = 4πr²ρε, and energy transport (radiative or convective) dT/dr. Plus a microphysics closure: equation of state P(ρ,T,μ), opacity κ(ρ,T), nuclear rates ε(ρ,T). That set + boundary conditions ⇒ a stellar model.

slides.title: Hydrostatic equilibrium + Virial scalings
slides.body:
**Hydrostatic equilibrium**: dP/dr = −Gm(r)ρ/r². Dimensional estimate (drop the integral): P_c ≈ GM²/R⁴. For the Sun: P_c ≈ 6.7×10⁻¹¹ × (2×10³⁰)² / (7×10⁸)⁴ ≈ 10¹⁶ Pa (10¹¹ atm). The actual central pressure from solar models is ~2.5×10¹⁶ Pa — order-of-magnitude correct.

**Virial theorem** (for a bound, ideal gas): 2K + U = 0, or kT_c ~ GM·m_p/R. Sub R = R☉, M = M☉ ⇒ T_c ~ 10⁷ K. The fact that hydrogen fusion ignites at T ~ 10⁷ K and gravity sets exactly that scale at solar mass is why the Sun is on the main sequence — it's not a coincidence.

slides.title: Nuclear fusion: pp-chain vs CNO cycle
slides.body:
**pp-chain** (dominant for M ≲ 1.3 M☉): 4 ¹H → ⁴He + 2e⁺ + 2ν_e + 26.7 MeV. Rate-limiting step: p + p → ²H + e⁺ + ν_e via the weak force (slow — the Sun's core would burn out instantly if it were strong). Energy per kg of H: 6.4×10¹⁴ J/kg. Mass-energy efficiency: 0.71% (Δm/m).

**CNO cycle** (dominant for M ≳ 1.3 M☉): C, N, O act as catalysts; same net 4p → ⁴He. Sensitivity to temperature: ε_pp ~ T¹⁷⁵, ε_CNO ~ T¹⁸ — CNO is ~10× steeper. Implication: massive stars have **convective cores** (the steep ε(T) creates a temperature gradient too steep for radiation alone). Low-mass stars: radiative core, convective envelope.

slides.title: Derive the Sun's main-sequence lifetime
slides.statement: Estimate how long the Sun can stay on the main sequence by burning H in its core. Assume ~10% of solar mass is in the core and available for fusion.

steps.prompt: What fraction of the rest-mass energy is released when 4 ¹H fuse into ⁴He? (Use atomic masses: 4×1.00784 u → 4.00260 u.)
steps.hint: Compute Δm/m, then multiply by c².

steps.prompt: How much total energy is released if 10% of the Sun's mass burns? (Use M☉ = 2×10³⁰ kg, c² = 9×10¹⁶ J/kg.)
At the current solar luminosity L☉ = 3.8×10²⁶ W, how many seconds is that?
steps.hint: Just divide; then convert seconds → years (3.15×10⁷ s/yr).

steps.prompt: The standard quoted MS lifetime for the Sun is ~10 Gyr. Why is our estimate within ~10%?
steps.answer: We assumed constant L (it actually rose from ~70% L☉ in the Hadean to today) and a constant 10% burnable core mass (the actual MS endpoint uses a more refined Chandrasekhar-type core mass). Both effects roughly cancel for a Sun-like star — for higher-mass stars the L grows so fast that t_MS shrinks as M^−2.5 even though L grows as M^3.5.
steps.hint: Think about what we held constant.

slides.prompt: Why does the CNO cycle dominate over the pp-chain in stars more massive than ~1.3 M☉?

choices.label: CNO releases more energy per fusion reaction (higher Q-value).
choices.rationale: Wrong — both net reactions are 4p → ⁴He + 26.7 MeV. The pathways differ but the Q-value is the same.

choices.label: CNO has steeper temperature dependence (ε ~ T¹⁸ vs T⁴ for pp-chain), so it wins at hotter cores.
choices.rationale: Correct. Massive stars have hotter cores (T_c ~ GM·m_p/R·k, and R grows slower than M), and the steeper ε(T) of CNO crosses over pp-chain near T_c ≈ 17×10⁶ K — corresponding to M ≈ 1.3 M☉.

choices.label: Massive stars have more C, N, and O — the catalysts.
choices.rationale: Massive stars have similar metallicity to lower-mass stars from the same cluster; the catalysts are not depleted. It's the temperature, not the C/N/O abundance, that matters at the cross-over.

choices.label: pp-chain needs neutrinos to proceed; CNO doesn't.
choices.rationale: Both pp-chain and CNO produce neutrinos (and rely on weak-interaction steps). Neither 'needs incoming neutrinos.'

slides.workedSolution: At T ≈ 1.5×10⁷ K (solar core), ε_pp ~ T⁴ outpaces ε_CNO ~ T¹⁸ because the CNO normalization is too small. Around T ≈ 1.7×10⁷ K, the CNO curve catches up; for any hotter star (i.e., M > 1.3 M☉), CNO dominates. The steepness of T¹⁸ also drives convective cores in CNO-burning stars.

slides.prompt: You observe a star with T_eff = 30,000 K and L = 50,000 L☉. Which structural feature is most likely to differentiate it from the Sun internally?

choices.label: It burns helium in its core via the triple-α process.
choices.rationale: He-burning happens later (red supergiant phase). On the main sequence even hot O-type stars are still H-burning, just via CNO.

choices.label: Its core is convective (because CNO ε~T¹⁸ creates a steep gradient that radiation can't carry).
choices.rationale: Yes — this is an O-type ZAMS star. Hot core ⇒ CNO dominates ⇒ ε(T) so steep that radiation alone can't carry the flux, so a convective core develops. Energy is mixed efficiently; the H-burning region is well-stirred.

choices.label: It has no nuclear fusion — it's powered by gravitational contraction (Kelvin-Helmholtz).
choices.rationale: K-H lifetimes are millions of years, not the ~10⁷-yr MS lifetime of an O star. Stars on the MS are unambiguously fusion-powered.

choices.label: Its mean molecular weight μ is much higher (~4 vs ~0.6) because it's helium-rich.
choices.rationale: A normal Population I O star has the same composition as the Sun — μ ≈ 0.6. It's been H-burning for at most a few Myr; no time to enrich.

slides.hint: Use the L–M and T–M scalings to estimate mass, then think about how the fusion regime changes.
slides.workedSolution: L ~ M^3.5 ⇒ M ≈ (50000)^(1/3.5) ≈ 30 M☉. Massive ⇒ hot core ⇒ CNO ε ~ T¹⁸ ⇒ steep gradient ⇒ Schwarzschild instability ⇒ convective core (~30% of the mass mixes). This is one of the qualitative signatures of upper-MS stars and a key input to stellar-evolution codes (mixing length theory, overshoot parameters).

slides.prompt: A star has mass M and radius R. Using the Virial estimate kT_c ≈ G M m_p / R, compute the central temperature in K for M = 20 M☉, R = 6 R☉. Take G = 6.67×10⁻¹¹, M☉ = 2×10³⁰ kg, m_p = 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg, R☉ = 7×10⁸ m, k = 1.38×10⁻²³.
slides.hint: T = G M m_p / (k R). Just plug in.
slides.workedSolution: GMm_p = 6.67×10⁻¹¹ × 4×10³¹ × 1.67×10⁻²⁷ ≈ 4.46×10⁻⁶. kR = 1.38×10⁻²³ × 4.2×10⁹ ≈ 5.8×10⁻¹⁴. Ratio ≈ 7.7×10⁷ K — close to the actual T_c of a 20 M☉ ZAMS star. (The factor-of-2 from real models comes from the integral form vs the dimensional estimate.) Acceptable answers around 3-8×10⁷ K.

slides.prompt: Why is the existence of stars at all such a remarkable cosmic accident? In ≤120 words, explain what would happen if the strong-force coupling were 5% stronger or 5% weaker.
rubric: Mentions hydrostatic balance: T_c set by gravity scales as G M m_p / k R.
Notes pp-chain rate-limiting step is weak-force (p+p→²H+e⁺+ν), which is slow — sets the stellar lifetime.
Stronger strong force → diproton (²He) is bound → 2p → ²He instantly, no slow weak step → Sun burns out in seconds.
Weaker strong force → deuteron unbound → no fusion ladder starts → no main sequence at all.
Either way, no long-lived stars ⇒ no time for chemistry, planets, biology. (The 'fine-tuning of the strong force' argument; see Carr-Rees 1979, Adams 2008.)
